body:
> - When this FileDialog is shown, I can still close the main window.
> - Calling file_dialog.show() multiple times lets me open multiple FileDialog windows.
> - file_dialog.visible always returns false, even when this FileDialog is open.

These are expected limitations. While some of this can be implemented on Windows, it's not possible on macOS and Linux, native file dialog is part of system process and can't be accessed in any way once shown (for security reasons, since file dialog can access files outside the sandbox). And controls usually have behavior as similar as possible on all platforms.

This is a deal-breaker because if using native file dialogs allows users to open multiple dialogs at once, it could break the program when the `file_selected` signal is emitted multiple times (mostly when opening and loading files).

I considered using Godot's custom file dialog, but it feels harder to navigate, and I often get lost in the directories (though this could be a matter of personal preference).

Godot's Editor FileDialog feels easier to use, but according to the [documentation](https://docs.godotengine.org/en/stable/classes/class_editorfiledialog.html), you can only use it in editor plugins.

> These are expected limitations.

So how are native file dialogs supposed to be used in practice then? And why did the behavior change between recent releases?

In 4.3, on Windows, the dialog would block the main window and prevent unexpected interactions with it until the user chooses the path or cancels the dialog. This is the expected behavior from, arguably, every piece of software. On my Linux machine the dialog does not block the main window, but it at least remains on top of it, making it harder to misplace it (small graces, eh).

In 4.5 (and I assume in 4.4 from this report) it no longer blocks the main window on Windows, and it quickly goes into background when you focus the main window. There is no system indication that the dialog is there (since it does try to be transient), it just exists somewhere behind all other windows you interact with. And naturally the user can then spawn multiple dialogs from your application, and that leads to issues, bugs, and possibly crashes that need to be handled somehow.

If this regressive change has been done on purpose, for parity, I'm confused what utility native file dialogs provide then. Since with the current implementation they lead to unexpected situations for developer and users (and that includes the Godot editor itself, by the way).

And then the parity argument is somewhat unconvincing, if I'm being honest. Is it really impossible to support on every modern OS? Obviously, it's possible to block the main window on Windows, that worked in 4.3. And while 4.3 didn't do that on my Linux (PopOS) laptop, other apps are capable of blocking the window when a native file dialog appears. Chromium and VS Codium to name a couple. That leaves Wayland (which I assume is separately relevant) and macOS. I can't test how Godot behaves on macOS, but other apps can definitely block the main window when the dialog shows.

So are you sure this isn't just a regression from some change?

> In 4.3, on Windows, the dialog would block the main window and prevent unexpected interactions with it until the user chooses the path or cancels the dialog. 

It was blocking the main thread, not just window, which was extremity buggy.

> On my Linux machine the dialog does not block the main window

It's entirely controlled by desktop environment, and not always the case.

> other apps are capable of blocking the window when a native file dialog appears

Only apps using built-in dialog of the widget toolkit they are using can be blocking, like Godot do with its built-in dialog, but it's not possible with system dialogs.

But I guess it would make sense to emulate blocking to the extent it can be (real blocking and forcing on top on macOS and Windows, and only blocking input on Linux).

I believe you are correct. The main window of VS Codium on my PopOS machine can be resized and moved around while the file dialog is open, and it reacts correctly to these changes. But input doesn't pass through to any internal part of the UI. And the app can still be closed, naturally (which is one of the complaints in the OP here).

I think that's acceptable for parity's sake.
